labctl.notes: EMULATED MACHINE, CONTAINED, NO CHECKPOINT: SIMH's PDP-10 (KS10) simulator runs MIT ITS inside a systemd-nspawn container together with the station's Xvfb and one xterm; the daemon captures the X root (SH_CAPTURE=x11) and types over XTEST (SH_INPUT_BACKEND=x11test). There is no pointer — this is a terminal exhibit. No QMP and no exec channel: `labctl shot` reads the X root. The visitor line is DZ11 line 0 on the CONTAINER's loopback port 10004, so it is unreachable from labhost; to drive the guest by hand, enter the container's netns — `nsenter -t $(cat /data/vms/streamhost/stations/its/mame.pid) -n telnet 127.0.0.1 10004` — and only while no visitor is attached. mame.pid is the SIMH pdp10 HOST pid (idle freezer and reap-by-exe), nspawn.pid the supervisor. The simulator console is NOT the museum surface: it goes to work/emulator.log and carries the `sim>` escape prompt. Reset=relaunch: kill pdp10 by mame.pid, wipe work/, copy the pristine rp0.dsk back and start again. Launcher stations/its/x11-runtime.sh, which execs the lane's shared engine stations/its/shared-terminal-runtime.sh; assets in assets/its (MANIFEST.sha256 pins the built tree).

museum.lineage: CTSS (MIT, 1961) → ITS on the AI Lab's PDP-6 (1967) → ITS on the PDP-10 → the hacker culture, Emacs and the GNU project that grew out of it
museum.arch: DEC PDP-10 (KS10 model, 36-bit words) under SIMH — an RP06 disk pack holding the whole system, and a DZ11 terminal multiplexer with the visitor on line 0
eraSoftware: DDT — the debugger MIT used as its command shell, so 'the shell' and 'the debugger' were the same program
Emacs, written here by Richard Stallman and Guy Steele as a set of TECO macros
TECO, the editor Emacs was built on top of
Maclisp — the Lisp that Macsyma, Emacs's successor and Scheme all came from

MIDAS, the PDP-10 assembler ITS itself is written in
museum.periodBrowser: none — ITS predates the web by two decades. Its network was the ARPANET, and this exhibit is deliberately not networked at all
museum.blurb: The operating system the word 'hacker' was invented around. MIT's AI Lab wrote ITS for its PDP-6 in 1967 in deliberate opposition to the Multics project down the hall: where Multics was security, accounting and a committee, ITS had no passwords, no file protection and no way to stop another user reading your terminal — on purpose, because the people on the ninth floor of Tech Square trusted each other and wanted the machine open. Emacs was written here. So were TECO, Maclisp, the INFO manuals, Zork's ancestor and most of the culture that became free software; Richard Stallman was ITS's last system administrator, and he started GNU because the machine that replaced it wouldn't let him fix the printer driver. The command processor is DDT, a debugger — on ITS you do not run a shell, you talk to the machine.
museum.notes: Tier 3, EMULATED but CONTAINED and with no checkpoint: SIMH's PDP-10 (KS10) simulator, the station's Xvfb and the visitor's xterm all run inside one systemd-nspawn container (private PID/mount/net/IPC/UTS/user namespaces, uid base 2424832, volatile overlay root, the built tree bound read-only, CAP_SYS_ADMIN dropped, mount syscalls filtered). ITS has no passwords and no protection between users — that is the exhibit, not an oversight — so the container, not the guest, is the security boundary. There is no media to source: the maintained github.com/PDP-10/its tree assembles the entire system from its own sources by booting a PDP-10 and building ITS inside it, and the RP06 that falls out is the exhibit (pinned in assets/its/MANIFEST.sha256). The visitor surface is one xterm on DZ11 line 0; the simulator console is never on screen. SIMH answers for itself from the ini file, so the simulator is the single supervised process and the station needs no pty/expect supervisor — the shared heritage-terminal runtime vax43bsd proved. No checkpoint: reset is a relaunch from the pristine built RP06. See docs/guests/its.md.

network.note: No network plane and no retronet reservation. ITS spoke ARPANET NCP and Chaosnet; neither has anywhere to go here, the DZ11 terminal line is the whole visitor surface, and the station is an island on purpose. The DZ telnet listener lives on the container's own loopback behind --private-network, so it claims no host port and is unreachable from labhost.

reset.mouse: N/A — no pointing device. A DZ11 terminal line carries keystrokes only, and the exhibit publishes no pointer (stream.pointer.present=false).
